blocks.text: **The problem.** You are given an integer array `nums` of length `n` where every value is in the range **1 to n**, and each value appears **once or twice**. Return every value that appears **twice**. The follow-up asks for **O(n) time** and **O(1) extra space**.

blocks.alt: The array [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]. The two 2s and the two 3s are highlighted, so the answer is [2, 3].

elements.text: Find All Duplicates in an Array

elements.originalText: n = 8, every value is between 1 and 8

blocks.code:
Input:  nums = [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]
Output: [2, 3]

Input:  nums = [1, 1, 2]
Output: [1]

Input:  nums = [1]
Output: []

blocks.text: The answer can be returned in any order. Keep an eye on the unusual promise — **values from 1 to n in an array of length n**. The best solution depends on it completely.
Compare each element with every element after it. Because a value appears at most twice, every matching pair is a different duplicate, so each one is reported exactly once.
**Time O(n²), space O(1).** The inner loop is asking one question over and over: *have I seen this value before?*
2. Optimal: remember what you've seen in a hash set
A hash set answers "have I seen this value?" in O(1). Walk the array once: if the value is already in the set, it's a duplicate; otherwise add it.
**Time O(n), space O(n).** Fast, but the set can grow to n entries, and the follow-up asks for O(1) extra space. Where else could we keep one "seen" mark per value?
3. Best solution: use the array itself as the "seen" set

Every value `v` is between 1 and n, so it can point at an index: its **home**, `v − 1`. That gives every possible value its own slot in the array. To mark "I've seen v", make the number stored at its home **negative**.

Walk the array once. For each value (read with `abs`, since it may already have been flipped), look at its home: if the number there is **already negative**, this value was seen before — it's a duplicate. Otherwise flip it to negative.

blocks.alt: The array [4, 3, 2, 7, 8, 2, 3, 1]. The first 3, at index 1, points to its home index 2 and flips it negative. The second 3, at index 6, points to the same home, finds it already negative, and is reported as a duplicate.
blocks.caption: Value v lives at index v − 1. A negative number there means "v has been seen".

blocks.text: After one pass, the signs tell the whole story:

blocks.alt: After the pass the array is [-4, -3, -2, -7, 8, 2, -3, -1]. Negative slots mean the value slot + 1 was seen. Slots 4 and 5 stayed positive, so 5 and 6 never appeared.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1)** extra. The "seen" marks live in the signs of the input. If the caller needs the array unchanged, flip every value back to positive in a second pass — still O(n).

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n²) time, O(1) space. Optimal: O(n) time, O(n) space. Best: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: **Read with abs()** — by the time you reach an element, it may already have been flipped negative by an earlier value.

blocks.text: The same "value points at an index" trick finds the **missing** numbers too: after the pass, every slot that is still positive is a value that never appeared (here 5 and 6). It only works because the values are limited to 1..n — always check the constraints for that hint.
